extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism scholars, journalism students, and newspaper editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for producing literary (narrative) newswriting — when to use scene, voice, tense, reporting methods, sourcing, and ethical limits. Emphasizes techniques that preserve factuality while achieving literary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration versus scene (present action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between narration (summary of events) and scene (present action that reproduces the movement of life); the scene lets the reader 'see how something happened' rather than read that it happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surmelian's examples contrasted; scene is present action (not merely present tense). Use scene to show process and motion; prefer scene when you can reconstruct and confirm events so the reader experiences the action unfolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of present tense for immediacy and poetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Present tense can increase a story's immediacy and poetic value, placing the reader inside a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sager's barn lead. Use present tense when it enhances sensory immediacy, but be mindful of accuracy and context (present tense is a stylistic choice, not a substitute for reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show process rather than merely summarizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer showing the process (how events unfolded) over summarizing that they occurred; the reader should be able to 'watch the action unfold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shinoff's gravedigger scene exemplifies showing process. Use scene to make a story more interesting; use summary only when it tightens the story, supplies necessary context, or when events are insignificant to merit dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and requirement for confirmations
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing a scene often privileges one subject's point of view; when adopting a subject's POV the writer must bring confirmations that the scene actually occurred that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's not enough to write a convincing scene; the reporting/documentation must support it. Verify who saw what and corroborate key details to avoid misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative approach as method for explaining 'how'
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative techniques allow journalists to shift from the factual 'what' to the more revealing 'how' of events without diminishing journalistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Lottinville notes, historians and journalists use narrative to tell how something happened; applying literary technique to 'how' can enhance usefulness to readers if backed by solid reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness and authority of the reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of narrative journalism depends on the trustworthiness of the writer; an untrustworthy writer transforms the work's total effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and maintain credibility through accurate reporting, transparent methods, and avoidance of invention or deception. The writer's authority must be established by demonstrable reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama and scene as defining factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama and scene (showing life in motion) are central to literary newswriting and can be prerequisites for attempting the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an event lacks drama or uncovered scenes, consider conventional reporting instead. Use scene and drama when they genuinely exist and can be documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place scene over information
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene should not trump essential factual information; no good newspaper journalist would prioritize scene above accurate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scene to create sensory representation and to enrich reporting, but ensure that the story still conveys necessary facts and allows readers to evaluate information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid credibility-boosting devices that mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute detail and vivid description can act as 'credibility-boosting devices' that imply a reporter's omniscience and may mislead if not supported by reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of using detail to imply conclusions beyond what reporting supports. Sproule warns against using dramatic detail to give false impressions of comprehensive knowledge; avoid mixing unsubstantiated analysis with reconstructed scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology as unfolding time (not merely past tense)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using chronological organization, treat chronology as unfolding time to show process and causal sequence rather than as a mere past-tense recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lottinville's advice: chronology can reveal cause/effect and reduce the writer's burden of argument, letting events demonstrate relationships where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of adjectives, adverbs, and rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary newswriting permits and often requires evocative adjectives, adverbs, metaphors, and other rhetorical devices to provide detailed sensory description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Doris Wolf's funeral scene. Use descriptive language to evoke more than mere facts, but avoid making evaluative claims unsupported by reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony must arise naturally from facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony can appear in literary newswriting but must emerge from events and facts rather than be imposed by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present ironic juxtapositions via documented detail and scenes (Drake on Hinckley). Avoid labeling things ironic or manipulating facts to create manufactured irony, as that risks compromising neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of summary/exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary and exposition remain valid tools when they tighten the narrative, provide context, or address events not significant enough to dramatize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booth and Shinoff examples: switch between dramatization and summary as function requires. 'Function decides form' — use exposition to move quickly over secondary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited and purposeful use of direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotations should be used when they show dialogue or reveal character; otherwise they may impede narrative flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature writing's reliance on 'good quotes' is contrasted with literary newswriting's tendency to reduce quotation use. Use quotes selectively for impact rather than as primary evidence of voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration only when necessary and non-self-centered
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration is permissible but should not turn the story into the journalist's self-revelation or advocacy; the reporter's presence should serve the story's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gilbert Gaul's coal-miners piece is an exception where the writer's role freed impressions. Use first person sparingly and only when immersion or participation materially enhances understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginnings must be compelling and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings must be both compelling and directly relevant to the story; they cannot begin wherever the writer feels like it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads like Sager's barn or opening murder scenes must hook the reader while accurately introducing the story's subject and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings must flow logically and sustain mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings should flow logically from the facts and do more than merely stop; they should sustain or conclude the story's mood or point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Drake's 'He fired.' or Crewdson's 'Bernabe Garay was a happy man at last.' Effective endings cap or extend the narrative feeling without inventing resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid style over substance; prohibit fabrication and dishonest composites
rubrics_metrics.description: Misuse of literary techniques — fabrication, invented scenes, or deceptive composites — is condemned and damages journalism's credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite high-profile abuses (Janet Cooke, problematic Carpenter passages). If a factual hole cannot be honestly filled, admit it rather than invent. Distinguish acceptable illustrative reconstructions from fraudulent fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of attribution and sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of attribution tags or unattributed reconstructions raise questions about credibility; readers rely on source identification to evaluate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include preface statements, lists of sources, footnotes or modified footnotes, or in-text reminders of basis for material. Boston Globe draft policy and Stockton Record labeling are cited as possible models. Some anonymity is acceptable but must be handled responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority comes from quality of reporting and immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of a literary news story derives not from rhetorical flourish but from immersion and the demonstrable quality of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norman Sims and others: immersive reporting that shows the author's work underpins credibility. Authority should be evident in the depth and rigor of reporting, not merely in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive reporting and documentation are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruction and literary techniques must be based on extensive reporting and documentation; documentation is essential to factual narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston Globe draft: reconstruction should be based on reporting, with someone present (preferably more than one) having notes or clear memory. Examples show reporting time ranging from one day to a year; reporters should 'know five times as much as you're ever going to use.' Use FOIA and records where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use events that can be verified or observed in progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Any event that a reporter can verify or observe in progress can provide a suitable basis for a literary framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: smuggling of aliens, digging graves, funerals. Prefer topics where reporting can corroborate descriptive scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function decides form
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice between literary technique and conventional reporting is dictated by what the reporting dictates — form should serve function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reporting reveals scenes suitable for dramatization, use them; if not, use conventional forms. The structure should arise from the story's informational and narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction should disclose constraints and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should clearly and honestly state the constraints and reconstruction methods under which a story was compiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edward Jay Epstein's suggestion: explain how material was selected and processed. Possible practices: statements that a story was 'reconstructed from interviews and trial transcripts' or short methodological notes embedded in or adjacent to the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation is required to distinguish factual narration from fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual narration aims to be true to history and requires documentation; fact and fiction may be on a continuum, but documented reporting anchors narrative journalism in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics cited: factual narration 'must be true not only to human experience... but to history.' Ensure archival, documentary, or multiple-source support for reconstructed scenes and assertions.
